summary:
ARTEMIS-IV is an interactive 3D lunar habitat simulation built in Roblox Studio that transforms real historical NASA space weather data into high-stakes survival and operational gameplay. Anchored at Shackleton Crater on the lunar South Pole during the historic May 8–15, 2024 solar superstorm, players take on the role of Artemis astronauts managing base telemetry, solar power grids, and daily crew routines across an 8-day mission cycle.

Integrated directly with the NASA Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information (DONKI) API, the simulator reproduces 138 chronological solar events—including Solar Flares (FLR), Coronal Mass Ejections (CME), and Solar Energetic Particle (SEP) radiation storms. Each phenomenon triggers realistic environmental hazards and emergency protocols: recalibrating damaged roof communications antennas during X-class flares, engaging magnetic shielding before CME plasma impacts, and retreating to radiation shelters during proton storms while monitoring oxygen, nutrition, and suit shielding. By turning raw astrophysical telemetry into an immersive, experiential training environment, the project bridges the gap between complex heliophysics data and public spaceflight education for future lunar exploration.
details:
Overview & How It Works ARTEMIS-IV: Lunar Space Weather Survival & Operations Simulator places players inside a multi-module lunar research outpost located at Shackleton Crater (89.54° S, 0.00° E). Without Earth's protective magnetosphere and atmosphere, lunar crews face direct exposure to space weather. Our simulator synchronizes with real chronological telemetry from the NASA DONKI API covering the extreme solar storm period of May 8–15, 2024 (138 real solar events), dynamically driving base systems, environmental effects, and crew survival tasks.

Core Gameplay & Space Weather Mechanics

  • Multi-Monitor Telemetry Command Center: Four real-time terminal displays render NASA DONKI bulletins, environmental sensors (lunar external temperature, cabin pressure, proton flux, and magnetic field stability), base safety status, and a dynamic daily Shift Checklist (06:00–18:00 UTC).
  • Solar Flares (FLR — M-Class & X-Class): Triggers electromagnetic interference across communications and HUD telemetry, causes interior base lighting fluctuations, and—during extreme X-class events—damages the rooftop communications antenna, requiring players to perform an EVA climb to recalibrate it before a total radio blackout occurs.
  • Coronal Mass Ejections (CME): Alerts the crew to incoming magnetized plasma waves. Players must engage Base Safety Mode and retract solar arrays at the command terminal before impact to prevent magnetic overload and life-support failure.
  • Solar Energetic Particles (SEP): Generates high-energy proton radiation storms. Players must monitor their suit's radiation shielding on the HUD and take shelter inside the shielded radiation module until proton flux normalizes.
  • Power Grid & Life Support Management: Players inspect three independent solar arrays via an interactive diagnostic terminal (monitoring operational status, motor state, and kW output) while managing crew nutrition, oxygen, and rest cycles in the dormitory to advance across the 8-day mission.

Tools, Technologies & Architecture

  • Engine & Language: Roblox Studio and Luau (client-server architecture separating authoritative server mission/NASA event orchestration from responsive client HUD and terminal interactions).
  • Data Pipeline: DonkiService module parsing and chronologically sequencing historical NASA DONKI JSON datasets (FLR, CME, and SEP classifications, UTC timestamps, and severity levels).
  • UI/UX Design: Custom NASA-inspired dark-blue and cyan terminal interfaces (SurfaceGui and ScreenGui) designed for high readability under emergency alert states.

Benefits & Intended Impact By gamifying authentic heliophysics datasets, ARTEMIS-IV turns abstract solar storm metrics into intuitive cause-and-effect experiences. Students, educators, and space enthusiasts learn how solar flares, CMEs, and radiation storms directly affect lunar infrastructure, communications, power generation, and astronaut safety—fostering awareness of the operational challenges ahead for NASA's Artemis program.
